fields.Front: Why is plate tectonics compared to the theory of evolution?
fields.Back: Because in both cases what had seemed a diverse set of almost random observations could suddenly be explained by a relatively simple, coherent theory. Plate tectonics was as important to earth scientists as evolution was to biologists.

fields.Front: What does plate tectonics explain, for three different audiences?
fields.Back:
Geological engineers: why and where significant deformation of Earth's surface occurs (where not to build a bridge).
Economic earth scientists: the type and location of many metallic mineral deposits.
Hazards: the global distribution of earthquake and volcanic hazards (though timing and magnitude remain trickier).
It also produces continents, ocean basins and mountain ranges.

fields.Front: What three lines of evidence did Wegener use for continental drift?
fields.Back:
1) The 'jigsaw fit' of the continents across the Atlantic - so good that coincidence was impossible.
2) The fit of glacial terrain on the southern continents when reassembled (otherwise Palaeozoic glaciers would have grown near the equator and across oceans).
3) Continuity of old geological structures and fossil stratigraphy (plants and animals) from continent to continent.

fields.Front: Why did few people immediately accept Wegener?
fields.Back: It was radical and revolutionary to believe landmasses had moved around and were still moving under their feet, and Wegener had absolutely no idea of the mechanism required - so people waited for more evidence.

fields.Front: How did World War II contribute to plate tectonics?
fields.Back: In the early 1940s, to detect sunken ships and lurking submarines, very sensitive magnetometers were towed in pods behind ships back and forth across sections of ocean. As well as steel hulls, they detected curious, repetitive magnetic records in ocean-floor rocks - but the data could not be processed until the war ended.

fields.Front: What did post-war ocean-floor mapping discover, and who made the famous map?
fields.Back: Two lines of research (hunting mineral resources, and simply mapping ocean floors) produced the first comprehensive ocean-floor maps from the late 1940s through the 1950s - the Tharp and Heezen panorama. In the Atlantic they defined a huge volcanic ridge running from the far north and connecting with similar ridges in the far south, volcanically active along almost its whole length: the largest volcanic system anyone had ever seen.

fields.Front: What exactly did Hess propose in 1960?
fields.Back: That mid-ocean ridges are SPREADING CENTRES where Earth's crust moves in opposite directions like conveyor belts, allowing new ocean floor to be built from volcanic rock at the ridges.

fields.Front: If new crust forms at ridges, why isn't Earth's surface area increasing?
fields.Back: Because old crust must be destroyed elsewhere - at subduction zones. (There were some pretty hot arguments about this in the late 1960s and early 1970s.)

fields.Front: How do you calculate a spreading rate from the sea floor?
fields.Back: Measure the distance from the ridge centre to a particular strip of basalt, date that basalt, then distance divided by time = rate of spreading.

fields.Front: List the key scientists of plate tectonics in order with their contributions.
fields.Back:
Wegener 1912: continental drift, Pangaea, no mechanism.
WWII naval scientists, early 1940s: towed magnetometers detect magnetic patterns.
Tharp and Heezen, late 1940s-50s: ocean-floor maps, mid-ocean ridge.
Hess 1960: sea-floor spreading.
Vine and Matthews 1963: symmetrical magnetic stripes.
Benioff and Richter, mid-1950s: seismographs, descending slab.

fields.Front: What did the WWII magnetometers actually detect, besides the magnetic patterns in ocean-floor rock?
fields.Back: They were glorified metal detectors, particularly sensitive to the magnetic anomalies of hunks of steel (sunken ships) and to the powerful generators needed to run submarines and ships.

fields.Front: Give the timeline of plate tectonic theory in one sequence.
fields.Back: Wegener 1912 (drift, Pangaea, no mechanism) -> WWII magnetometers (early 1940s) -> ocean-floor maps and the mid-ocean ridge (late 1940s-50s) -> Hess 1960 (sea-floor spreading, 2.5 cm/yr, 180 Myr) -> Vine and Matthews 1963 (symmetrical stripes) -> Benioff and Richter (subduction from earthquake foci) -> mantle plumes and slab pull.

fields.Text: {{c1::Alfred Wegener}} published continental drift in {{c1::1912}} and named the supercontinent {{c1::Pangaea}}, but his theory's weakness was that he had no {{c1::mechanism}}.

A {{c1::magnetometer}} measures {{c1::magnetic field strength}}; sensitive ones were towed behind ships in the early {{c1::1940s}} to detect sunken ships and submarines, and accidentally recorded {{c1::ocean-floor}} magnetism.

In {{c1::1960}} {{c1::Harry Hess}}, a professor at {{c1::Princeton}}, proposed sea-floor spreading; he calculated the Atlantic widens about {{c1::2.5 cm}} per year (fingernail growth rate), putting the continents in contact {{c1::180}} million years ago.
Plate motion is watched in real time with very accurate {{c1::GPS}} units fixed to continents, whose satellite-measured positions shift a few {{c1::centimetres per year}}.
The supercontinent Wegener pictured in his jigsaw fit was called {{c1::Pangaea}}; the slides note it began breaking up in the {{c1::Jurassic}}.
